phase.label: Anhui years, 1667: a young Chan monk

source.label: Wikipedia: Shitao moved “to Anhui in the 1660s”; Met: painted in 1667 at the age of twenty-five

highlight.text: Mei Ch'ing (1623-1697), a master painter of a generation before, [inscribed] the painting with praise for Tao-chi's skill, noting that the artist worked on the almost twenty-foot scroll for a full year.

work.text: In Tao-chi's [entertaining] depiction of the theme, the lohans are shown reading scriptures, meditating with a tiger, discoursing on Buddhist law as they stroll with a fantastic beast (ch'i-lin), and, at the center of the composition, witnessing with wonder and fascination the emergence of an electrifying dragon from the bottle of the “dragon tamer” lohan

source.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
source.title: Tao-chi, Sixteen Lohans
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Recent Acquisitions: A Selection 1985–1986 (Internet Archive scan)

work.text: Shitao’s powerfully built beast with its hate-filled humanoid eyes is realistically threatening. Its long, flapping, snakelike tail whips up a tidal wave of cosmic vibrations: rising ocean breakers, angry [spidery] tree branches, and massive rock outcroppings with throbbing contour lines and struggling “veins” or “arteries,”

source.author: Wen C. Fong
source.title: Wang Hui and Repossessing the Past
source.publisher: in Maxwell K. Hearn (ed.), Landscapes Clear and Radiant: The Art of Wang Hui (1632–1717), The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: In a colophon at the end of [The Sixteen Luohans], Mei Qing (1623—1697), a close friend of Shitao, identifies Li Gonglin (ca. 1041—1106) as the source of the [artist’s] “monochrome-outline” (baimiao) technique … But Shitao probably never saw an original work by a real Song master.

source.author: Wen C. Fong
source.title: Wang Hui and Repossessing the Past
source.publisher: in Maxwell K. Hearn (ed.), Landscapes Clear and Radiant: The Art of Wang Hui (1632–1717), The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: According to Buddhist doctrine, the Buddha ordered sixteen guardian lohans to live in the mountains while awaiting the coming of Maitreya, the Future Buddha.

source.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
source.title: Tao-chi, Sixteen Lohans
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Recent Acquisitions: A Selection 1985–1986 (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: As a descendant of the Ming imperial family, Tao-chi's life was imperiled at the time of the Manchu conquest in 1644. He was raised in Buddhist monasteries and, in 1662, became a disciple of a powerful Ch'an master, Lu-an Pen-yueh (died 1676). … Yet, even in 1667, his clear devotion to the Buddhist faith, manifested in this scroll, was overshadowed by his exuberant talent and dedication to his [craft].
